title: Article 2 — Admission or establishment of new States

content.overview: Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. It is the gateway for external admission or creation of States that are not formed by reorganisation of existing States under Article 3.
content.glance: Parliament may by law admit or establish new States on terms it thinks fit. Distinct from Art 3 (reorganisation of existing States).
content.study:
Article 2:
‘Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.’

Scope:
- Admission: bringing a territory/political unit into the Union as a State (historically relevant to integration of princely States and later admissions such as Sikkim’s full statehood path).
- Establishment: creating a new State otherwise than by the internal reorganisation modes listed in Article 3.

Terms and conditions: Parliament has wide latitude to prescribe the terms of admission or establishment.

Relationship with Article 3: Article 3 deals with formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States (internal reorganisation). Article 2 is the complementary power for admission/establishment. Both are implemented by ordinary parliamentary law; Article 4 allows such laws to amend the First and Fourth Schedules and provides that they are not amendments under Article 368.

Procedure: Ordinary legislative process (no special Article 368 majority). Where a law under Article 2 amends the First Schedule, Article 4 applies.

sections.heading: Constitutional text
sections.body: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.

sections.heading: Admission vs establishment vs Article 3
sections.body: Admission/establishment (Art 2) concerns bringing in or creating a State that is not merely carved from or altered among existing States. Article 3 covers formation of a new State by separation of territory from any State, uniting two or more States or parts, uniting any territory to a part of any State, and alteration of boundaries or names. In practice, major reorganisations have used Article 3; Article 2 remains the textual basis for pure admission/establishment powers.

sections.heading: Exam checkpoints
sections.body:
1. Quote Article 2 fully.
2. Distinguish Article 2 (admit/establish) from Article 3 (form/alter existing).
3. Note Article 4: Schedule amendments; not Article 368 amendments.
4. Parliament’s power as to terms and conditions is wide.

examples.title: Illustration — Admission on terms
examples.body: Parliament admits a territory as a new State under Article 2 and, by the same law, amends the First Schedule (Article 4) and specifies transitional terms. The law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

misconceptions.trap: Every new State requires an Article 368 constitutional amendment.
misconceptions.correction: Laws under Articles 2 and 3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules under Article 4 and are expressly declared not to be amendments under Article 368.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Article 2 of the Constitution.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. It is distinct from Article 3, which deals with formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States. Laws under Article 2 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules (Article 4) and are not amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

examTips: Always distinguish Art 2 (admit/establish) from Art 3 (reorganise existing). Cite Art 4 for Schedule changes.
